about.title: About Giovanni De Gattis
about.description: Where I'm from, what I work on now, and how I went from motion design to building product full-time.
about.mainHtml:
Back
Updated May 20263 min read

A bit about me

Designer, Developer, Cook

I've always been a builder. People have asked me what it is that I enjoy doing, and my response is always "making things." Not the best answer, but it holds.

In school I was the kid making custom slide decks while everyone else used the templates, mostly because the templates were ugly and boring. That hasn't really changed. If something catches my eye, I want to know how it works, then I want to make one myself.

The medium doesn't matter much. Whether it's code, designs, or chef knives (one day I will be a blacksmith).

I built a Shopify store and the brand around it for a family friend's spice business, and she loved it. That's the bit I keep chasing: delight. Everything I make has to feel good, work well, or ideally both.

I grew up in Kincardine, a small town on the Ontario lakeshore. Before that, Ottawa. Going from the city to a rural farming and tourist town was odd at first, but Kincardine is lovely, and so are the people.

What stuck with me is the dark. Walking home from a friend's house at night with no streetlights, just the wind in the trees and the complete certainty that nothing was about to bother you. The safety of nature's always been a thing that calls to me.

I camp at least once a year. Usually Tobermory, sometimes Algonquin. The portaging trip I did in school is still the best week I've had outdoors, moose and all. My working life is mostly screens, and the place I feel most settled is a tent. Funny how that works, but I suppose it's not too uncommon.

My current favourite is the Moritaka Ishime mega nakiri in Aogami #2. Moritaka has been forging blades in Kyushu for around 500 years, starting with swords. It's heavy carbon steel, so it rusts if I leave it wet, and it holds an edge in a way I didn't really believe until I owned one. The first time I used it, I drove it a touch too deep into the cutting board, which really shocked me. One would think that such a brutalistic tool would be a burden to use, but it is surprisingly nimble!

I aspire to achieve that level of finesse in the things that I create.

My first knife was a gift: a Yu Kurosaki Senko Ei gyuto in SG2 powder steel. Kurosaki became Japan's youngest certified master blacksmith, earning the title in his forties. It's a beautiful, slightly absurd object. It's my everyday knife, and it's borderline indestructible.

What I love about Japanese knives is that they sit on this odd line between simple and impossibly exact. People spend generations refining a single profile and still find more to learn. I haven't tried forging one yet. But I will. And it will be glorious.

For now I tell myself I'm "still in the exploring other knives" phase, which is a handy excuse for buying more of them.

avatone.title: Avatone · Giovanni De Gattis
avatone.description: A gamified fitness app that I design and build full-time. Avatars, rewards, friendly competition, and positive growth. All free, with a thriving playerbase.
avatone.mainHtml:
Back
Updated July 20262 min read

Avatone

Flutter, Figma, Rive, Framer, TypeScript

Owning the whole loop

I work closely with our CEO, Parsa, deciding what Avatone needs next. Once a feature is mine, I research it, design it, build it, and refine it. I have final say on UI and UX, while Ramy owns merge approval and technical quality. Victor shapes the artwork, and Danny handles the audio.

Avatone is a fitness app built around avatars and rewards. More than 70,000 lovely people have joined so far.

That button everyone kept pressing

The first iteration of our onboarding demanded an answer to every question. Firmly. Designed as though the users actually wanted to answer every question, rather than diving straight into the app. This was a pain point, as evidenced by users in our session replays hammering the disabled “continue” button on every screen.

We rebuilt the panels around the avatar, let people skip non-essential fields with sensible defaults, and finished with a 1,000 Grit reward (in-app currency) to spend on basic cosmetics. It became playful, quicker, and easier to understand.

Case Study Following the drop-off

Making the number trustworthy

Working between Flutter, Mixpanel, and Supabase really taught me a lot. All these intricacies for stable and reliable tracking across platforms. Our funnel was lying to us at first: an app restart counted the same person as both a failed attempt and a fresh start. I fixed the tracking logic and batched our events before I trusted the numbers enough to judge the work.

What changed

Completion rose from roughly 60% during Avatone's first few thousand users to a 70% average across over 70,000 folks. This comparison spans the product's evolution. Several releases contributed to the lift.

Still shaping it

I use the same loop across the product and everything else that I touch: watch what people do, find the friction, make the change, then measure. Avatone keeps making that problem more interesting.

brutalist-poster-study.title: Brutalist poster study · Giovanni De Gattis
brutalist-poster-study.description: Four posters made for no one but me. Midjourney pitched the image, I did everything else.
brutalist-poster-study.mainHtml:
Back

Brutalist poster study

Midjourney, Figma, Type, Poster Design

Off the clock

Client work pays the bills, and it’s mostly tidy. Phone screens, sensible flows, problems with a right answer. I wanted something expressive with no brief behind it, so I followed an itch. Moody, chunky, colourful posters had been filling my Pinterest for weeks, the kind where gothic type sits straight over a photo and the subject pushes through the letters.

Ideation, not implementation

The references all share one move. The title is huge and the subject passes in front of it, so the word and the image fight for the same space. The brutalist ones add their own grammar on top: desaturate the photo to near-duotone, allow exactly one acid colour, blunt grotesque or gothic type, barcodes, tally bars, a column of credits no one reads. Yellow for the ruined tower, red for the bandages, orange for the monument.

Midjourney handed me the subjects and nothing else. You can generate something that looks good. You cannot, at least not yet, generate a well laid-out graphic. For the layout I drove Figma through its MCP with Claude Fable, the best available as I write this, and nothing could position a poster properly. It managed the odd accent, then fell apart the moment it had to place a mask or another visual with any care. The state of the art wasn’t enough. Good for ideation, terrible for implementation. I think that speaks volumes. So the layout, the restraint, and the masking where the subject cuts through the type all stayed with me.

I like making things

I don’t want to be the person who only does simple phone UI. I like making things. All the things. This was one of them, put together between jobs with no one to please, and it turns out that’s sometimes exactly what you need.

I refined the four that called to me and left the rest. Most of the batch I just wasn’t feeling, and that’s allowed when nobody’s waiting on it.

buzzfeed-ux-redesign.title: Buzzfeed UX Redesign · Giovanni De Gattis
buzzfeed-ux-redesign.description: UX course project at Carleton: untangling Buzzfeed's chaotic navigation. Clear hierarchy over engagement tricks.
buzzfeed-ux-redesign.mainHtml:
Back

Buzzfeed UX Redesign

Figma

The pick

For a UX class at Carleton, we had to take an existing site and redesign it properly. I picked Buzzfeed because I’d grown up on it and, surprisingly, it hadn’t gotten much better. The navigation is a mess of competing elements, unclear categories, and inconsistent branding. You don’t know if you’re reading actual news or a quiz about what type of bread you are.

What changed

I redid the whole main flow: navigation, sibling sites, content separation. Spacing did a lot of the heavy lifting. Once articles and quizzes and video weren’t crammed into the same dense band, the rest of the work got easier. Trending got room to breathe. Partner sites like Tasty stopped pretending to be the same product. I leaned on how the Guardian and BBC pace their feeds for reference, then wrote a long report defending every choice.

How it landed

A hi-fi clickable prototype, a thick written report, ninety-five percent and a tutor who seemed genuinely surprised. Still tucked toward the back of the portfolio, since it’s older. But the bones held up.

d2ttk.title: D2TTK · Giovanni De Gattis
d2ttk.description: A Destiny 2 weapon roll simulator, built over a weekend as an experiment, now a popular web app.
d2ttk.mainHtml:
Back
Updated July 20262 min read

D2TTK

Astro, TypeScript

A weekend replacement

I have around 6,000 hours in Destiny 2. When D2Foundry shut down, the community lost its weapon-roll and time-to-kill tool. An integral piece when it comes to PvP video games. I gave myself a weekend to build the core again as an experiment.

That first release had a weapon database, TTK calculations and lookup by name, perk or source. It worked. Since then, my solo build has gained browse functionality, data updates, shareable rolls, a shooting range, and further improvements.

Correcting the source

Bungie’s API contains incomplete (and sometimes incorrect) gameplay values. I cross-check community tables, Discord feedback, and my own audits. As an example, there’s a perk called “Elemental Capacitor”, which gives an advantage based on whatever element you’re using. In Bungie’s data, it just incorrectly assumes you are using all elements at once, tremendously inflating its impact.

Calculations start with decimal damage against 230 health (the normal amount a player should have). Regression tests cover the timing paths where a tiny mistake may change the answer.

Case Study Browse beat the search box

Search came first

Search and dropdowns worked for players who knew what they wanted. Everyone else needed to see what existed first.

Adding browse

I added every weapon to a browse view. Analytics showed far more repeat visits there than on search. It makes sense, really. The previous UI was for people who KNEW what they were looking for. A browse view gives a sense of discovery and exploration.

Where it stands

Early traffic was around 100 visits a day. D2TTK now sees 1,000 to 3,000 a day and has held around 24,000 monthly users.

Back to top

gradients-fyi.title: gradients.fyi · Giovanni De Gattis
gradients-fyi.description: A free OKLCH mesh-gradient editor. Grain, blur, liquify, dither, and no subscription for a blurry blob.
gradients-fyi.mainHtml:
Back
Updated July 20262 min read

gradients.fyi

Next.js, WebGL2, OKLCH, TypeScript

One week to a renderer

Most mesh-gradient tools charged for the useful parts (primarily exporting), so I built one for my own work. Building the renderer took about a week. Its first usable version could build meshes, adapt palettes, stack layers, and export images.

Underneath is raw WebGL2 with radial basis interpolation and colour processing in OKLCH and OKLAB. Colour interpolation is my favourite part. Colours stay bright through the middle instead of collapsing into the dull band a straight RGB blend often produces.

A tool I still reach for

Inside the editor are mesh, linear and orb gradients, with grain, blur, liquify and image export. Its layout borrows a useful idea from Figma: canvas in the middle, controls beside it, every point to be moved directly by hand.

On the homepage, an endless stream of randomly generated gradients explains the tool through its output, while also making it easy to blast through them for inspiration.

Case Study Keeping the colour alive

Hue wraps

Hue is circular. A direct blend can take the long way around the wheel or snap where 360 degrees becomes zero.

Sine and cosine

Each hue becomes sine and cosine values before interpolation, then returns to an angle with atan2. That gives the shader a smooth short path without a seam.

Where it appears

These gradients appear throughout my work and in Avatone's branding and pitch decks. Around 50 people visit each day. I still use it myself.

Back to top

immigration-canada-web-app.title: Immigration Canada Web App · Giovanni De Gattis
immigration-canada-web-app.description: Summer co-op at IRCC. Built document filtering and sharing tools for the people processing immigration cases.
immigration-canada-web-app.mainHtml:
Back
Updated July 20261 min read

Immigration Canada Web App

Vue, TypeScript, C#, Full Stack

Making a document tree useful

My first development co-op was with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada. Staff used an internal platform to find forms while assisting immigrants and refugees. At the start, it was essentially a tree of documents.

My assignment let staff save, group, and share those documents across teams. I designed the interface, presented it to my manager and team, then worked directly with the platform’s proprietary C# API and file data types.

Case Study Rebuilding while learning

Switching to Vue

Midway through the term, the frontend moved to Vue. Learning it on the fly meant rebuilding my work inside the government's own architecture.

Handing it off

My feature reached review. Then my placement ended. Its release happened after I left, so I don't attach an adoption number, but I do know that it was a substantial upgrade, impacting every single user of the platform.

What stayed with me

What stayed with me was learning a real system quickly enough to contribute, and then learning how to carry it over into a completely different framework.

jaune.title: JAUNE · Giovanni De Gattis
jaune.description: A fake archive of one-of-one shirts that don't exist. Everyone I showed it to thought it was real, and a few were gutted they couldn't buy in.
jaune.mainHtml:
Back
Updated July 20261 min read

JAUNE

Astro, Tailwind, Midjourney, Concept

Concert visuals, heavy cotton

A Joji concert put the first idea in my head. Those visuals kept escalating, and I had recently fallen for heavy (200+ GSM) cotton T-shirts. I started wondering what a one-off fashion archive would look like if every shirt became more expensive than the last.

Its economics were half art project, half joke about NFT hype. With enough attention, I still think somebody would have tried it.

Building the fiction

I directed the concept, wrote the prompts, assembled the collection, and built the site. Midjourney made the images. I am not the artist, and the project is clearest when that credit is explicit.

Each piece is treated as a sealed 1/1 edition, with a real domain and an archive that gets dearer as it empties. Checkout was deliberately absent. A too-convincing shop would invite someone to buy, then disappoint them.

People believed it

Around 3,000 people visited during the first week, before I had told anyone about it. Friends and strangers assumed the brand was real. A few wanted to buy a shirt and were disappointed when they found out there was nothing to ship.

Visual direction, pricing, and small details made an imaginary label feel plausible.

Back to top

kanso.title: kanso · Giovanni De Gattis
kanso.description: Nine Claude Code skills for people who think AI-generated code is too long. Delete before you add, earn every line.
kanso.mainHtml:
Back

kanso

Claude Code, Plugin, Code Quality, Open Source

Deleting the same five things

Claude writes working code, then buries it. A comment narrating every line, null checks on values the types already guarantee, and a try/except that swallows the error and returns None. One security firm audited 300-plus repos and found tautological comments in nearly all of the AI-written ones. I was deleting the same five patterns from every diff, so I wrote the deletions down and made them load before the model types anything.

Tautological comments, filler, silent errors 
def get_user(user_id):
    # Fetch user by ID
    try:
        result = db.query(User).filter(User.id == user_id).first()
        if result is not None:
            return result
        else:
            return None
    except Exception as e:
        return None
def get_user(user_id):
    return db.query(User).filter(User.id == user_id).first()

Nine ways to say less

kanso (簡素, elimination of clutter) is a Claude Code plugin. The core skill is a standing set of anti-dilution rules that loads automatically: comments must explain why rather than echo the code, and an abstraction waits until the third concrete case. Around it sit eight commands for auditing, refactoring, committing and writing PRs, all with the same curatorial bias. The audit reports before it edits, the refactor never mixes cleanup with behaviour change, and a hook lints every touched file the moment it changes. Anything that writes is manual-only.

Defensive programming theatre 
def process_order(order: Order) -> Invoice:
    try:
        if order is None:
            raise ValueError("Order cannot be None")
        if not isinstance(order, Order):
            raise TypeError("Expected Order instance")
        try:
            total = sum(item.price for item in order.items)
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Error summing items: {e}")
            return None
        return Invoice(order_id=order.id, total=total)
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Unexpected error: {e}")
        return None
def process_order(order: Order) -> Invoice:
    total = sum(item.price for item in order.items)
    return Invoice(order_id=order.id, total=total)

The deleting habit

Building it changed how I read my own code. I now spot a filler variable from across the room, and I have caught myself writing commit messages that answer why instead of what, which the plugin nags about anyway. The taxonomy will drift as models do. Half of it will need rewriting within a year, and that’s fine. Git remembers.

Back to top

mimesis.title: mimesis · Giovanni De Gattis
mimesis.description: Six Claude Code skills that strip the machine fingerprint from writing. Zero em dashes, ever.
mimesis.mainHtml:
Back

mimesis

Claude Code, Plugin, Writing, Open Source

The fingerprint

Every model writes the same way. The em dash pairs, the “not X, but Y” pivot, the sentence that ends by underscoring its own importance. Wikipedia’s AI Cleanup project has catalogued these tells across thousands of flagged articles, and once you’ve read the list you can’t unsee it. I was hand-editing the same patterns out of everything Claude drafted for me, including the copy on this site, so I turned the editing pass into a plugin.

Negative parallelism, kill-list words

This isn't just a design system - it's a journey. By leveraging a robust set of shared tokens, we unlocked seamless collaboration across the entire ecosystem, highlighting the transformative power of a common language.

The design system started as a spreadsheet of hex codes. Once the tokens lived in code, designers stopped pasting values into Slack and the front end stopped drifting. The shared language did the rest.

Guidelines outrank the model

mimesis (μίμησις, imitation) is six skills with one thesis: the quality lives in a versioned corpus of tells and a deterministic linter, not in whichever model happens to be writing. The linter is a single Python script with no dependencies. It flags em dashes as blockers, catches the en-dash and double-hyphen workarounds, and scores prose for flat rhythm and narrow vocabulary. The kill list is versioned by model era because the tells drift. There’s also a compile skill for the opposite job, writing dense instructions for a machine reader, where the tells are fine.

Puffery without evidence

Jane is a passionate, results-driven engineer with a proven track record of delivering innovative, scalable solutions that empower teams to achieve their full potential.

Jane builds payment infrastructure. She rebuilt the reconciliation system twice, once wrong, once less wrong, and writes about what the second attempt taught her. Based in Edinburgh.

Imitating a person

There’s an obvious irony in asking Claude to remove Claude’s own tells, which is exactly why the rules live in files the model can’t argue with. The linter false-positives sometimes, and I’ve made peace with that; it reports, a human decides. What I haven’t made peace with is how many em dashes I used to write myself. Apparently the machine learned them from us.

Back to top

model-bench.title: Model Bench · Giovanni De Gattis
model-bench.description: Side-by-side LLM comparison tool. Pick your models, stream responses, let an AI judge score them.
model-bench.mainHtml:
Back

Model Bench

Next.js, Tailwind, Cloudflare Workers, Hackathon

The wall

Not everything I make has AI in it, but enough does that the same question keeps coming up: which model should I actually use? There are comparison tools baked into various platforms, but nothing standalone, nothing free, and nothing that lets you throw a real task at a stack of models with your own files and prompts.

I just wanted that.

How it works

Pick your models, write a prompt, optionally upload files and schemas, hit run. Every model streams its response side by side, colour-coded so you can tell them apart. When they finish, an AI judge (Claude Sonnet 4.6 by default, but you can swap it) reads the responses blind and scores them on accuracy, clarity, and completeness. The judge shuffles responses before scoring so a model isn’t punished for being in the wrong column. Scores accumulate on a leaderboard across runs. Cost per response tracked down to fractions of a cent.

Under the hood

Next.js 16 with App Router, Tailwind, Framer Motion. OpenRouter as the gateway, which gives one API key access to every provider. Deployed on Cloudflare Workers, squeezed under the 2 MiB limit. No database, no auth, no sign-up. Paste a key and go.

The interesting bit was the streaming. One browser request fans out to several models on the server, and each model’s tokens have to make it back through a single stream tagged correctly. Each model gets its own fetch on the server, every chunk gets stamped with the model ID, and the client splits them apart on arrival. If the user closes the tab, every upstream fetch cancels cleanly. Took longer than the rest of the app combined.

The hackathon turned out to be a scam, which I learnt after putting most of my time into the build. A small group was lifting ideas and stretching the timeline until they got caught. Model Bench just kept being useful. A few hundred people a month use it now, mostly me.

Back to top

ocd-psa.title: OCD PSA · Giovanni De Gattis
ocd-psa.description: A personal PSA about living with OCD. Messy, uncomfortable, deeply personal first-year design work.
ocd-psa.mainHtml:
Back
Updated July 20262 min read

OCD PSA

Adobe Illustrator, Figma, Procreate

You are not your thoughts

This first-year brief asked us to make a PSA for a Canadian charity. The Canadian Mental Health Association gave me room to address OCD, something I have lived with since childhood.

The single most impactful quote that I have ever heard in my life: “you are not your thoughts.” Intrusive thoughts are central to OCD, yet that part is rarely explained well. Once I understood the difference between having a thought and believing it, I could grapple with the condition differently.

Finding the image

One early direction put a head inside a birdcage. It communicated being trapped, but missed the cruelty and noise of intrusive thoughts. Mouths worked better. They became voices sitting on top of the person, saying things that feel close while remaining separate from them.

My professor liked the direction and asked for more expression. I exaggerated the mouths, pushed their shapes, and vectorised the finished piece.

A student piece I kept

The work never ran as a public campaign, so there is no reach metric attached to it. It stays here because even though it was one of the first things that I made, I remain proud of its expression and purpose.

Back to top

repshare.title: RepShare · Giovanni De Gattis
repshare.description: Social fitness app concept that eventually became Avatone. Designed during university between classes.
repshare.mainHtml:
Back

RepShare

Figma

Before Avatone

Second year of my IT and design degree, a message landed in our programme’s public Discord. Parsa, my now-boss, needed a designer and couldn’t pay. I was the only one to respond. I needed portfolio pieces. He needed help. A fair trade.

That’s how RepShare started.

The idea

The pitch was simple: going to the gym with your friends instead of going to the gym and texting your friends. Most fitness apps punish you for falling off track. We wanted something where your mates pulled you back in. “Hey man, let’s go. You’d better not flake.”

We worked on it off and on between classes. Login, home, chat, calendar, profile. The profile screen still holds up.

What became of it

RepShare never launched under that name, but it didn’t die either. It shifted focus, picked up gamification and an actual attitude, and grew into what Avatone is today. RepShare was the idea. Avatone is the real one.

Glad I answered that Discord message.

Back to top

sunshine-clementine.title: Sunshine, Clementine! · Giovanni De Gattis
sunshine-clementine.description: Solo wellness journal that maps weather to mood over time. Full-stack course project, A+ in a live defence.
sunshine-clementine.mainHtml:
Back

Sunshine, Clementine!

Django, React, ShadCN, Figma

The concept

Culminating project for a full-stack course, solo build. A wellness journal that tracked how the weather lined up with your mood over time. Open it, tap how you’re feeling, write a sentence to future-you. Quick, no friction. The OpenWeather API ran in the background, and everything else lived in a local Django database. ShadCN had just dropped at the time and barely anyone was using it, which is why the whole interface is built around it.

Defending it

The course finished with a live oral exam. The professor sat across from us and asked us to modify features in real time: swap an API, change the weather logic, walk him through the codebase, explain a decision out loud. Intimidating in theory. In practice it was clarifying. You either understood your own code or you didn’t, and you found out fast. A+, and he seemed pleased.

What showed up in the data

Watching patterns emerge in test data was the best part. Seasonal dips that lined up suspiciously well with the calendar. The app wasn’t trying to fix anything, just remind people that what they’re feeling isn’t happening in a vacuum.

If I built it now, post-Avatone, I’d give it more whitespace and far fewer features. Less is generally more. But I was very proud of this one.

Back to top

the-space-between.title: The Space Between · Giovanni De Gattis
the-space-between.description: A horror game that listens to your heartbeat and uses it against you. Capstone project, fourth at Level Up.
the-space-between.mainHtml:
Back

The Space Between

Unity, Figma, C#, OpenGL

Capstone

Four years of school came down to one project, and the grade was the difference between graduating and not. The Space Between is a psychological horror game built around your heartbeat. The game listens, adapts, and uses your pulse against you through a custom peripheral we built.

I was lead developer and designer. In practice that meant the enemy AI, the player movement, the procedural camera sway, every UI screen, the navigation, the objectives, the music I composed, the SFX I chose, the heart-rate logic, and the website you’re about to click through to. Most of the game’s feel passed through my hands at some point.

Case Study Wiring up a heartbeat

The hook

The pitch was one line: a horror game that uses your heartbeat against you. Easy to say. Much harder to get stable enough for a capstone demo on a judge we'd never met, in a room full of interference.

The peripheral

A 3D-printed enclosure, an Arduino, a pulse sensor, some soldering. Raw pulse streams into Unity. A secondary smoothing pass drops the spikes without killing the swings, which is the signal that actually matters.

What the game does with it

Elevated heart rate nudges world state: faster pathing, sharper audio, thinner margins. Not a difficulty knob. The scariest thing isn't the monster speeding up. It's realising afterwards that it did, because you got scared. The loop has to feel hidden or it stops working.

The technical side

A boids algorithm for the mimics, which spawn as chairs in places chairs shouldn’t be. Stand near one and it remembers it isn’t a chair. When the monster’s around, they swarm. Real-time custom background blurs in the UI through hand-written shaders. The monster ran two behaviour trees, switching context depending on which side of the world the player was in.

Case Study Two brains for one monster

Why two brains

A single FSM made the enemy predictable within ten minutes. Playtesters learnt the pattern and got bored, which in a horror game is worse than easy.

How they split

One brain handles the dark dimension where the monster lives. It tracks the player aggressively, lines of sight, noise, line-of-best-fit hunting. The other handles the other side, where it can't see you exactly. It predicts where you'll be. The handoff fires when you cross between worlds.

The one that stuck with me

The boids mimics. Emergent enough that I got jumped by my own game once, which I take as evidence it works.

Why horror

Horror has always pulled me in. Not the cheap scares, the slow dread. The feeling that something is slightly wrong. We wanted players to feel watched and to feel their own pulse betray them. I think we got there.

The project got an A, and later took fourth in its category at Level Up in Toronto. A proud way to close out school. The night before the demo, the website wouldn’t render and the build wouldn’t launch. I stayed up until five.

Back to top

tooth-and-nail-redesign.title: Tooth and Nail Redesign · Giovanni De Gattis
tooth-and-nail-redesign.description: First-year group redesign for Tooth and Nail, an Ottawa brewery. Bold branding, eased pacing, and beer later.
tooth-and-nail-redesign.mainHtml:
Back
Updated July 20262 min read

Tooth and Nail Redesign

Figma, Powerpoint

Giving the beer room to speak

This was a four-person first-year redesign for Tooth and Nail, a local Ottawa brewery. I led the research, built the interface and assembled our presentation deck. The group also included other designers and artists.

While some would argue the opposite, I am especially drawn to those hipster products with gorgeous branding and clean, beautiful sites (see Mana Yerba Mate as an example). In the case of Tooth and Nail, their site was the polar opposite of this. Which in itself is endearing in a way, but not a way that appeals to me.

The existing site had very little hierarchy. Products were hard to scan, prices disappeared, and the pages felt closer to forms than a brewery with a strong point of view. I built moodboards, reviewed competitors and turned the supplied type and colour into a small design guide before moving into wireframes.

Case Study Three decisions

Make the products obvious

Large product photography and visible pricing gave each beer a clear place to land. Big, beautiful product shots, especially when showcasing something bold, just make it pop and feel so much more worth looking at. They hired a talented artist for the cans, and showcasing their work was a tremendous improvement at zero cost.

Add some personality

A more structured page and better use of colour made the site feel like a brewery rather than a catalogue form.

Keep it clean

The owner responded well to the colour and simplicity. We learnt during the presentation that a professional redesign was already underway, so our version stayed a student concept, unfortunately.

Looking back

The visual work has been tidied since school, but the core decisions are the same: clearer products, calmer pacing and a much easier path to the price.

Back to top

uavpro-dashboard-design.title: UAVPro Dashboard Design · Giovanni De Gattis
uavpro-dashboard-design.description: First contract gig. Redesigned a drone training platform's dashboard for students, teachers, and admins.
uavpro-dashboard-design.mainHtml:
Back

UAVPro Dashboard Design

Figma

The mess

My first contract work, brought to me by my friend Luka, who’d been offered the gig and wasn’t sure where to start. UAV Pro had years of features piled on top of each other: chat, file storage, weather monitoring, classroom management, billing. All grown organically, no cohesion. We had a week.

Three users, one platform

The platform served three completely different people. Students checking assignments and weather before flights. Teachers managing classrooms and communications. Administrators overseeing everything. They needed different logic, not cosmetic variations.

I led the design. Weather widgets for pre-flight checks. Event planning for meetups. Project management with drag-and-drop file handling. Threaded messaging that didn’t feel like an inbox. Luka implemented from my references and I polished. The dashboard came out feeling like a command centre rather than a pile.

How it went

They loved it. Then the company collapsed, rebranded, and disappeared from view, so I’ll never know what shipped.

A useful first taste of contract work. Solve the practical problem cleanly, hand it over, get on with the next thing.

whodunnit-repo-monitor.title: Whodunnit Repo Monitor · Giovanni De Gattis
whodunnit-repo-monitor.description: A Mac app that breaks down who actually did the work in a git repo. The seed that grew into whowrote.dev.
whodunnit-repo-monitor.mainHtml:
Back

Whodunnit Repo Monitor

Swift, Python, Figma

The spark

A group project I poured everything into came back graded too low. The professor wasn’t budging. So I wrote Python to do the talking: commit counts broken down by type, because one teammate had been duplicating the entire project to inflate his contribution graph. I CC’d the professor’s boss. Then his boss’s boss. Each message had hand-coded visualisations attached.

The grade went from a B+ to an A.

Building it properly

While writing those scripts, I realised there wasn’t a clean tool for this. Around then I’d been getting into beautifully made Mac apps like Alcove, and I wanted something with that same care. So I learned SwiftUI from scratch and built Whodunnit: filterable contribution views, calendar selection, colour-coded contributors, commit dashboards, all scoped to any repo on your machine.

I never released it. Only I ever used it. It still lives on my laptop.

What it became

Whodunnit taught me that this data is genuinely useful and that the tools for visualising it are thin on the ground. A while later that same instinct, with the attitude turned down, became whowrote.dev.

Same root, kinder vibe.

Back to top

whowrote-dev.title: Who Wrote · Giovanni De Gattis
whowrote-dev.description: Spotify Wrapped for GitHub repos. Paste a repo, get a stack of shareable cards that tell you who actually wrote it.
whowrote-dev.mainHtml:
Back
Updated July 20262 min read

Who Wrote

Next.js, Tailwind, Framer Motion, Cloudflare Workers

A softer second version

Whodunnit began as a private Mac app after a school group project where my contribution wasn’t credited fairly. It did the forensic work, but its Swift app and Python dependencies made it awkward to share. Its name sounded like an accusation, too.

Who Wrote turns the same commit data into a web experience that anyone can open. I borrowed the pacing of Spotify Wrapped, and built a stack of themed cards that feels curious, rather than confrontational.

Turning commits into a story

Paste any public GitHub repository and the app builds a tailored and shareable set of cards from its commit history. It covers contribution share, streaks, changed lines, and working hours, then adds a few stranger observations so the results have some personality to them.

My hardest problem was making enough cards to create variation while keeping the load time reasonable. More than the data had to change. Fewer cards felt unremarkable, while too many became an overhaul. Keeping the format consistent lets colour and content carry the variation, while remaining understandable.

Case Study Matching the result to the repo

Different repositories, different cards

A solo project and a large team produce very different histories. A selector scores each card against the repository and drops anything empty or dull, so the cards stay meaningful.

My own repository

Running Avatone through it showed that I had contributed roughly 47% of its commits and changed lines. I joined initially as a UI and UX designer, so seeing that shift laid out in one card caught me off guard!

woodsmoke.title: Woodsmoke · Giovanni De Gattis
woodsmoke.description: Camping trip planner for Canadian parks. Weather, fire risk, gear lists, and the top 100 sites on one map.
woodsmoke.mainHtml:
Back
Updated July 20262 min read

Woodsmoke

React, Figma, Hackathon

Booking starts months early

Camping in Canada often means booking in April, then discovering the good sites are already gone. Weather is the second gamble. I have arrived for trips that turned into days of rain, and fire bans can change the plan just as quickly.

Woodsmoke puts the useful decisions on one map: campgrounds across Canada, expected weather, fire risk, bear-country notes and a packing list. I built the whole thing over one weekend for DeveloperWeek 2026.

A forecast for booking day

Most forecasts stop well before a campsite opens for booking. For each park, Woodsmoke combines Open-Meteo’s live outlook with five years of weather around the same dates. That produces a useful range, then the app turns it into clothing and cooking suggestions.

Its campground list mixes broad provincial coverage with the popular parks I could verify. Fast scanning mattered more than stuffing every campsite into the first version.

Case Study Weather beside the map

Why they belong together

A map answers where. Historical weather answers whether the trip still sounds pleasant. Keeping them together made the planning flow quick enough to use while comparing sites. This is genuinely a struggle my family and I experience annually, so this site's been a lifesaver.

After the hackathon

Woodsmoke didn't place, and I haven't touched it since submission. It still drew a few thousand verified visitors without any further work.

Back to top

animated-accordion.title: Animated Accordion · Giovanni De Gattis
animated-accordion.description: A native details element that glides open instead of snapping, with ::details-content.
animated-accordion.bodyHtml:
Can I change my plan?

Yes, whenever you like. Upgrades apply straight away and we credit the difference; downgrades take effect at your next billing date.

What happens when my trial ends?

You move onto the free plan automatically. Nothing is deleted, and we never start charging without asking first.

How do I cancel?

From Settings, in two clicks. Your account stays open until the end of the period you've already paid for.

Animated Accordion

Open the questions and watch the native details element glide between its closed and open states.

Turn the glide off to feel the difference. This keeps the interaction semantic while giving longer answers room to breathe.

button-hover-fill.title: Button Hover Fill Animation · Giovanni De Gattis
button-hover-fill.description: A button where the background fills from whichever edge the cursor enters. Direction-aware hover that feels physically intuitive.
button-hover-fill.bodyHtml:
Button Hover Fill Animation

Move into the button from different edges and notice where the colour begins before it spreads across.

The entry point makes a simple hover feel connected to your movement, a useful touch for calls to action and compact controls.

clip-path-hover-reveal.title: Clip-Path Hover Reveal · Giovanni De Gattis
clip-path-hover-reveal.description: Hovering causes a clip-path circle to expand from the cursor, revealing a different layer beneath. Follows the mouse in real time.
clip-path-hover-reveal.bodyHtml:
Not everything is as it seems

There's always more beneath the surface

Hover to reveal

A different perspective awaits beneath

Clip-Path Hover Reveal

Move across the panel to reveal the layer beneath your cursor, then try the invert control to swap which message sits on top.

A live clip-path reveal can add depth to a quiet surface without changing the layout underneath.

container-query-responsive-card.description: Drag to resize a single card and watch it reshape from horizontal listing to stacked card to minimal badge. Powered by container queries.
container-query-responsive-card.bodyHtml:
Studio Monitor
Flat response · 50 Hz – 30 kHz
£249
£249

Container Query Responsive Card

Every card here is asking one question: how much room do I actually have? Media queries can only answer with the size of the whole window, which is the wrong question when a card might live in a sidebar one day and a full-width list the next.

Container queries let the card measure the box it sits in, so the layout decision travels with the component. Drag the handle and watch it choose listing, stacked or badge all by itself.

css-hover-delay.description: Tooltips appear only after sustained hover using CSS transition-delay. No JavaScript timers needed.
css-hover-delay.bodyHtml:
Shared with
Broden Kelly Design Lead
Mark Bowen Engineer
Lee Kiernan Product
Adam Devonshire Marketing

CSS Hover Delay

Hover each avatar and pause to see its tooltip arrive after a short dwell.

Turn the delay off for an instant comparison. CSS transition-delay gives busy toolbars a little breathing room without timers.

css-hover-jitter-fix.title: CSS Hover Jitter Fix · Giovanni De Gattis
css-hover-jitter-fix.description: Side-by-side product cards showing how hover transforms cause jitter - and the parent-wrapper fix.
css-hover-jitter-fix.bodyHtml:
CSS Hover Jitter Fix

Hover both cards and compare the shaky boundary on the left with the steady lift on the right.

The fixed version keeps the hit area still while its child transforms, so the pointer does not chase a moving target.

cursor-proximity-grow.title: Cursor Proximity Grow · Giovanni De Gattis
cursor-proximity-grow.description: A macOS-style dock where icons magnify smoothly as the cursor approaches, using Apple's cosine-curve algorithm.
cursor-proximity-grow.bodyHtml:
Cursor Proximity Grow

Glide across the dock and notice how nearby icons grow before the cursor reaches them. A proximity curve makes a compact toolbar easier to scan while keeping every item in place.

cursor-trail-fading-clones.description: Cursor trail that spawns fading SVG clones on mouse move. Pure CSS animation, no canvas. Includes an aurora colour-cycling mode.

Studio Nova

We craft digital experiences

Design, motion, and interaction.

Cursor Trail with Fading Clones

Sweep across the panel to leave a trail of fading shapes behind your pointer. Try Aurora mode for a shifting colour treatment, a small touch that can make a hero feel more alive.

dropdown-safe-triangle.description: Invisible triangle between menu trigger and flyout lets you move diagonally without the submenu closing. The jQuery menu-aim trick, rebuilt from scratch.

Safe Triangle on Dropdown

Open 'Align to' and move diagonally towards the flyout. The invisible triangle gives your pointer a forgiving route, which helps menus stay open while people aim for a submenu.

grainy-gradients.title: Grainy Gradients · Giovanni De Gattis
grainy-gradients.description: A grain-dithered gradient that avoids visible colour stepping.
grainy-gradients.bodyHtml:
Grainy Gradients

Turn the grain on and off to compare a quantised gradient with its finished treatment. The off state makes the colour steps easy to spot. The enabled state restores the continuous gradient and adds a feTurbulence grain layer, the practical treatment that keeps a large colour field from feeling digitally flat.

holographic-card-shader.title: Holographic Card Shader · Giovanni De Gattis
holographic-card-shader.description: A trading card that tilts toward the cursor and catches the light with holographic foils drawn per-pixel by a WebGL fragment shader.
holographic-card-shader.bodyHtml:
Giovanni

@cadorowo

Holographic Card Shader

Hover the card and it leans with your cursor while the foil catches the light, the way a holo card flashes when you rock it under a lamp.

The finishes are a WebGL fragment shader on the card face. The tilt angle stands in for the viewing angle, so the shine sweeps against the card rather than with it, and head-on the card looks almost plain, just like the real thing.

On Prism, the portrait is printed over the foil so the rainbow engraving only hits the background, a trick borrowed from real holo cards.

Hover Intent Detection

Move slowly across the navigation to open a menu, then sweep past it quickly to see the difference. The velocity check protects menus from opening when someone is simply passing through.

hover-parallax-layers.description: A developer profile card with 5 parallax depth layers: dot grid, card surface, content, avatar, and floating skill pills, all shifting at different rates on hover.
hover-parallax-layers.bodyHtml:
London, UK

Alex Morgan

Product Designer

Crafting interfaces that feel alive

UI Motion Systems

Hover Parallax Layers

Move around the profile card and watch its layers drift at different speeds. Separating depth like this adds a little dimension while keeping the content readable and still.

landscape-depth-card.title: Landscape Depth Card · Giovanni De Gattis
landscape-depth-card.description: A photograph with cursor-driven scene depth and progressive blur.
landscape-depth-card.bodyHtml:
I go outside
and I feel free

Love yourself.

Preparing your view…

Landscape Depth Card

Move across the photograph to shift the scene inside its stationary frame. Focus the card and use the arrow keys to explore it, too.

Change photo cycles through seven scenes. Upload photo previews your own image locally.

Presets use precomputed depth maps, with no model download. Upload photo loads FastDepth (5.2 MiB plus its runtime) only when needed. Your image stays on your device. VGPU renders the parallax; browsers without WebGPU keep a still preview.

magnetic-cursor-snap.title: Magnetic Cursor Snap · Giovanni De Gattis
magnetic-cursor-snap.description: Buttons pull the cursor toward them within a proximity radius. Increases effective hit area with a smooth, spring-back feel.
magnetic-cursor-snap.bodyHtml:
Magnetic Cursor Snap

Move near the buttons and feel them lean towards your cursor, then pull away to watch them spring back. A gentle magnetic zone can make small actions easier to reach without making the buttons larger.

proximity-type-morph.title: Proximity Type Morph · Giovanni De Gattis
proximity-type-morph.fullHtml:
Proximity Type Morph

Move across the word and the letters grow heavier beneath your pointer. The effect stays local, so one part of a character can change while the rest keeps its original shape.

Each glyph has five matching vector weights. A 2 x 3 spring grid follows the cursor, then a Gaussian field blends the cells together. The SVG outlines, advance widths and kerning update in real time, so the word spreads naturally as it gains weight.

scroll-driven-reveal.title: Scroll-Driven Reveal · Giovanni De Gattis
scroll-driven-reveal.description: Reveal-on-scroll and a reading progress bar on the compositor, zero JavaScript.
scroll-driven-reveal.bodyHtml:
The quiet return of the sleeper train

Joe Talbot · Travel · 6 min read

Night trains were supposed to be finished. Budget airlines had eaten their routes, the rolling stock was ageing, and operators quietly wound them down one timetable at a time.

Then something shifted. Austria kept its network running while everyone else cut theirs, and the bookings kept coming.

A berth from Brussels to Vienna now sells out weeks ahead in summer, and the passengers are not nostalgics; most of them are under forty.

Part of it is arithmetic. A sleeper swallows the hotel night and the airport transfer in one ticket, and you wake up in the centre of town.

Part of it is quieter than that. There is a particular pleasure in watching a city slide past while you brush your teeth.

The operators have noticed. New carriages are on order across Europe, with proper mattresses and doors that lock.

Scroll-Driven Reveal

Scroll through the article and notice the reading bar advance while each paragraph arrives near the viewport. Scroll back up to see the reveal work in both directions.

The browser ties these effects to the scroller itself, so the page gets a sense of progress without a scroll listener. It is a good fit for short stories, case studies, and long-form reading.

self-drawing-lines.title: Self-Drawing Lines · Giovanni De Gattis
self-drawing-lines.description: A signature that draws itself with stroke-dashoffset, no path measuring script.
self-drawing-lines.bodyHtml:
Delivery note

Order #4821 · Received in good condition

Recipient signature 12 Jul 2026

Self-Drawing Lines

Watch the signature appear along the delivery note, then press Replay to start it again. The finished line remains visible for visitors who prefer reduced motion.

A normalised SVG path and stroke-dashoffset create the drawing effect without measuring the path in JavaScript. It works nicely for signatures, annotations, and small hand-drawn accents.

spotlight-cursor-effect.title: Spotlight Cursor Effect · Giovanni De Gattis
spotlight-cursor-effect.description: A dark overlay with a radial-gradient hole follows the cursor, creating a flashlight that reveals the content beneath.
spotlight-cursor-effect.bodyHtml:
The Quiet Craft of Digital Typography

How thoughtful type choices shape the way we read on screen

Good typography is invisible. When a typeface is well chosen, the reader forgets the letters and sees only the meaning.

"Typography is the craft of endowing human language with a durable visual form."

- Robert Bringhurst

Spotlight Cursor Effect

Move your cursor across the page and the dark layer opens around it, like a small torch over the typography.

The same idea can guide attention through a dense screen without hiding the content underneath.

spring-button-effects.bodyHtml:
Quick Actions

+ K

Spring Button Effects

Press Command or Control with K, or click the keys, and watch them squash and settle with a springy finish.

Switch to the flat style to compare physical depth with a simpler colour change for keyboard feedback.

staggered-hover-ripple.title: Staggered Hover Ripple · Giovanni De Gattis
staggered-hover-ripple.description: A music grid where hovering one tile sends a ripple of lift and glow outward to neighbours with staggered delay.
staggered-hover-ripple.bodyHtml:
Rabbit Run Rabbit Run
Danny Nedelko Joy as an Act of Resistance
Grounds Ultra Mono
Mother Brutalism
Television Crawler
I'm Scum Joy as an Act of Resistance
Mr. Motivator Ultra Mono
Gift Horse TANGK

Staggered Hover Ripple

Hover a track and the lift travels through nearby tiles, with each neighbour arriving a moment after the last.

Slow motion makes the delay easier to read, a useful way to give a grid a sense of direction without adding noise.

Sticky Hover Fix

Tap a song in the phone mock-up, then switch the media-query guard and try again to see the sticky hover state appear or disappear.

The guard lets touch feedback stay intentional while ordinary hover remains a desktop-only interaction.

default

::file-selector-button
Profile photo JPG or PNG, up to 4 MB

Styled File Upload

These two inputs are the same native control, with only the button on the right receiving a little CSS polish.

Pick a file to keep the browser-owned filename and accessibility behaviour in place while changing the visual treatment.

subgrid-column-alignment.title: Subgrid Column Alignment · Giovanni De Gattis
subgrid-column-alignment.description: A card grid where each card's internal elements align across cards using display subgrid, compared side-by-side without it.
subgrid-column-alignment.bodyHtml:
Sarah Chen
Lead designer with 8 years of experience in product design.
Marcus Williams
Full-stack engineer. Previously at Stripe and Vercel. Specialises in distributed systems and real-time data pipelines.
Aiko Tanaka
Product manager.

Subgrid Column Alignment

The cards share invisible rows, so descriptions of different lengths still leave every button on the same line.

Toggle subgrid off to see why ordinary card grids drift, then turn it back on when repeated content needs a common rhythm.

theme-aware-favicons.title: Theme-Aware Favicons · Giovanni De Gattis
theme-aware-favicons.description: Favicons that flip from black to white when the browser goes dark, using a media query inside the SVG itself.
theme-aware-favicons.bodyHtml:
Your repositories
The case for boring tools
Photos for everyone
github.com

Theme-Aware Favicons

Drag the slider through the three browser themes. With the effect off, all three favicons stay solid black, and on a dark or black tab strip they simply vanish. Turn it on and the same marks invert to stay legible.

The switch cannot come from your stylesheet, because a favicon is a separate file and your CSS has no reach into browser chrome. The media query has to live inside the SVG, which is why so many sites ship a black square and never notice.

tilt-card-perspective.title: Tilt Card Perspective · Giovanni De Gattis
tilt-card-perspective.description: A card that tilts toward the cursor using CSS custom properties updated on mousemove. Pure CSS perspective transform with smooth transitions.
tilt-card-perspective.bodyHtml:
CSSCONF 2026

Giovanni

Product Engineer

ON, Canada

ATTENDEE #0247

Tilt Card Perspective

Move across the badge and it leans towards your cursor, with the glare shifting to make the surface feel close to the light.

The angles are just CSS custom properties, a compact pattern for adding depth without a 3D library.

typewriter-text.title: Typewriter Text · Giovanni De Gattis
typewriter-text.description: A headline that types itself with a blinking caret, from the steps() timing function and the ch unit.
typewriter-text.bodyHtml:
$ npm run build

Typewriter Text

The command arrives one character at a time, with steps() keeping the reveal crisp and the caret blinking at the end.

Press replay to run it again, then reuse the same ch-based width for short status lines or terminal-style moments.
